column3: Places wealth and children under trial while locating the great reward with God.
Adds purposeless immersion as a mode of play, with an appointed encounter beyond it.
Offers only an ambiguous use of play, including a mixed route.
Joins worldly life, deferred full recompense, and its deceiving enjoyment.
Immediately qualifies the non-demand for wealth by exposing coerced asking and avarice.
Restates play and diversion while setting enduring life in the other abode.
Pairs the play-diversion judgment with the better abode for those who have taqwa.
Connects faith and obedience with preserving rather than nullifying deeds.
Shows guidance increasing and taqwa being given to the guided.
Makes worldly wealth and children a source of affliction rather than admiration.
Frames immersion and play as limited until the promised day is met.
Reinforces wealth and children as trial against a great reward with God.
Adds taqwa and patience against hostile reaction, not the wealth or play theme.
Continues the local argument: spending, withholding, human need, and divine self-sufficiency.
Relates faith to entrusted conduct but adds no direct wealth or recompense relation.
Expands play and diversion into adornment, boasting, accumulation, and worldly decay.
Supplies nearby context of deeds being nullified through following what angers God.
Contrasts claimed future wealth and offspring with an unsupported expectation.
Offers a limited economic boundary: ending exploitation does not erase principal.
Shows withheld bounty turning against its holder, clarifying the danger behind avarice.
Adds the warning that worldly life can deceive against God's true promise.
Links faith and taqwa to a great reward amid testing and differentiation.
Nearby assurance that deeds will not be diminished supports the reward clause.
Adds reward as receiving good and protection from harm, a parallel protective reading.
Clarifies the non-extractive pattern through guidance that asks no reward from hearers.
Nearby return from guidance through embellished delay only indirectly bears on diversion.
Pairs faith with continuing taqwa as a durable stance.
Places wealth among trials and recommends patience and taqwa.
Nearby contrast of rejecting revelation and deeds becoming void.
Links taqwa and patience with reward not being lost.
Sets transient worldly enjoyment against the lasting abode of settlement.
Nearby warning about turning away, corruption, and severed ties.
Treats wealth and selves as costly commitment, not the focus's non-demand.
Directly warns that wealth and children can divert from remembrance and produce loss.
Shows religion being treated as mockery and play; the route remains mixed.
Pairs faith and righteous deeds with an unwithheld reward; contrast route is boundary only.
Opposes wrongful consumption of wealth and permits consensual exchange.
Nearby consequence scene adds little to the focus's stated conditions.
Names the excellent reward of workers without developing the focus's condition.
Uses taqwa for repair and goodness, only indirectly parallel to 47:36.
Contrasts a claim of divine poverty with human wealth, but only at channel level.
Directly distinguishes a messenger's recompense from any demand on the audience.
Distinguishes asserted submission from faith entering hearts while preserving deeds through obedience.
Nearby call to knowledge, forgiveness, and believers gives broad faith context.
Exposes amassed and counted wealth as a distorted measure of security and value.
Adds non-coercive separation after unbelief, not the focus's reward or wealth relation.
Nearby disclosure through signs and speech does not develop 47:36 directly.
Shows a call to prayer recoded as mockery and play, though the route is mixed.
Links faith and taqwa to mercy, light, and forgiveness as layered enabling gifts.
Contrasts truth and falsehood; its play-channel resonance is only indirect.
Connects making religion play and diversion with worldly deception and forgotten encounter.
Addresses exclusive calling and faith without a usable link to the focus's themes.
Nearby promised entry into the garden is reward context only.
Reiterates the non-extractive messenger pattern; redundant with the earlier identical formula.
Ties treating religion as play and diversion to worldly deception and eventual accounting.
Nearby contrast of following falsehood or truth gives broad orientation only.
Provides contrast-only route evidence, not positive support for 47:36.
Pairs obedience with a good reward and turning away with punishment.
Makes withholding contagious through commanding others to withhold, while God is self-sufficient.
Its giving-related reading is mixed and not localized to the focus themes.
Uses taqwa in relational repair, a distant parallel to the focus's condition.
Nearby loss of deeds gives only general contrast.
Defines creation as not play, supplying a serious-purpose boundary for the focus's play language.
Shows loss being answered by better giving and forgiveness, a parallel non-extractive economy.
Nearby call to reflection and closed hearts bears only indirectly on diversion.
Reiterates reward belonging to the Lord rather than being requested from listeners.
Mentions faith and divine giving but adds no focused relation.
Security and falsehood evidence does not materially clarify 47:36.
The near-place and changing victory reading is too remote from the focus.
Directly treats immersion and play as no excuse for mockery of God, signs, and messenger.
Nearby testing of struggle and patience supplies broad trial context only.
Challenges wealth's presumed ability to rescue at collapse; mixed evidence remains secondary.
Questioning about the Hour adds no specific route to the focus.
Nearby opposition and annulled deeds offers only general contrast.
Presents giving wealth as purification, reversing the assumption that outflow is mere loss.
Knowledge of the Hour has no direct bearing on 47:36 here.
Nearby protection of believers gives broad faith context only.
Uses wealth in costly striving, a limited parallel to action beyond possession.
The bare mutual-questioning phrase offers no usable addition.
Nearby secret obedience to revelation's opponents is only indirect context.
Again separates the messenger's reward from audience payment, now redundant evidence.
Reinforces faith as an active response to a messenger's call.
Need and provision form a distant channel-level parallel to non-extractive giving.
Depicts play within doubt as delaying recognition; useful but narrower than the focus.
Promises rectified deeds and forgiveness after obedience, without the focus's core terms.
Nearby exposure of inward rancor does not clarify the focus's claim.
Distinguishes received provision from hoped-for divine bounty, a limited giving parallel.
Uses taqwa to sustain repair and mercy, an indirect parallel.
Shows enjoyment and extended hope becoming diversion from the approaching end.
Sets truth against play, marking play as the contrary of consequence-bearing speech.
Tail-audit card with no specific link to play, wealth, reward, faith, or taqwa.
Shows reward as conditional wage in another setting, a limited contrast to divine reward.
Pairs taqwa with gratitude after aid, only generally parallel.
Worldly ease and denial of the final encounter give a remote worldly-life contrast.
Identifies intense love of wealth as attachment that blocks its forward use.
Uses taqwa to favor generosity beyond legal minimum, an indirect outflow parallel.
Connects hearing guidance and faith with freedom from loss or burden.
Shows an unsupported claim of trust, only distantly related to faith.
Tail-audit conduct instruction has no direct interpretive addition here.
Pairs faith and righteous action with good recompense, but remains general.
Contrasts a request confined to worldly good with the wider horizon of the next life.
Holds worldly good and good in the next life together rather than treating them as one horizon.
Calls for spending before a final day when exchange and compensation fail.
Figures spending in God's way as multiplication, directly reversing loss through outflow.
Names wealth and children among attractive worldly desires while setting a better return with God.
Makes giving from what is loved a condition of reaching righteousness.
Frames action as exchange between worldly life and the next.
Explicitly calls worldly enjoyment little and the next life better for taqwa.
Contrasts worldly goods with the greater spoils held by God.
States that reward of this world and the next are both with God.
Contrasts taking the near worldly offering with expectation of forgiveness.
Lists wealth and family attachments that may outrank love of God and striving.
Condemns hoarding gold and silver rather than expending it in God's way.
Shows hoarded wealth becoming a burdening consequence for its holders.
Presents selves and wealth as given in exchange for the garden.
Portrays worldly life's flourishing as brief and suddenly cut down.
Links seeking worldly life and its adornment to full worldly payment.
Marks worldly-only work as losing value in the next life.
Names worldly enjoyment as slight beside the next life.
Describes preferring worldly life over the next and obstructing God's way.
Contrasts what passes away with what remains with God and joins patience to reward.
Links preferring worldly life over the next with a grave evaluative consequence.
Sets an immediate-worldly aim within a bounded, non-enduring allotment.
Pairs seeking the next life with faith and striving, whose effort is recognized.
Warns against turning toward worldly adornment away from remembrance.
Depicts worldly life as rapidly vanishing vegetation.
Calls wealth and children worldly adornment while lasting righteous deeds are better in reward and hope.
Introduces those whose effort is most lost despite their activity.
Locates that lost effort in worldly life while its holders suppose it good.
Forbids extending attention toward worldly splendor and names God's provision as better and more lasting.
Questions whether wealth and children necessarily mean hastened good.
Completes the warning that apparent worldly provision is being misread.
Calls worldly goods temporary enjoyment and reserves what is with God as better and more lasting.
Commands seeking the final abode through what God has given without forgetting one's worldly share.
Describes knowledge confined to the outward worldly life while heedless of the next.
Warns not to let worldly life deceive against the final day.
Denies that abundance of wealth and children establishes nearness or immunity.
Contrasts cultivation aimed at the next life with cultivation aimed only at this world.
Calls what people receive worldly enjoyment and what is with God better and more lasting.
Treats worldly luxury as temporary enjoyment rather than final value.
Links turning from remembrance with wanting only worldly life.
Commands spending from entrusted wealth while linking faith and spending to a great reward.
Distinguishes degrees among those who spend and strive before decisive change.
Uses the loan image for giving to God and promises multiplied return and generous reward.
Pairs charitable giving with multiplication and generous reward.
Shows preferring others over oneself despite need, a lived counterpoint to withholding.
Introduces faith and striving with wealth and selves as a saving exchange.
Specifies faith and striving with wealth and selves as the terms of that exchange.
Forbids trade from displacing the summons to remembrance.
Shows trade and amusement drawing people away from the communal summons.
Commands spending before death makes delayed giving impossible.
Joins taqwa, hearing, obedience, spending, and release from avarice.
Identifies an acknowledged due within wealth.
Extends that due to the requester and deprived person.
Names love of the immediate as a competing orientation.
Pairs love of the immediate with neglect of the next life.
Begins the contrast of transgression and preferring worldly life.
Explicitly names preference for worldly life as the decisive orientation.
Supplies the consequence for that worldly preference.
Begins the contrary orientation of fearing standing before God.
Supplies the consequence for restraining desire in view of that standing.
Explicitly names preference for worldly life.
Calls the next life better and more enduring.
Begins the sequence of giving and taqwa.
Adds affirmation of the best to the giving-taqwa sequence.
Promises facilitation toward ease for that sequence.
Begins the contrary sequence of stinginess and self-sufficiency.
Adds denial of the best to that contrary sequence.
Promises facilitation toward hardship for that contrary sequence.
Names intense love of wealth as a controlling attachment.
Names rivalry in accumulation as diversion.
Extends that diversion until graves are reached.
